title: The Aurès to the Well of the Queen: the Mountain, the Fire, and the Mantle After
years: c. 645-703 (traditional; the war years c. 688-703 attested in broad outline)
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: The Aurès, born to the Jarawa
stops.campa: In the high country of the Aurès, among the Jarawa of the Zenata confederation, a girl is born to the chief the tribe remembers as Tabet, or in another remembering, as Matiya son of Tifan, Matthew son of Theophanes. The tradition gives her no fixed day, only the mountain: goat-paths, oak scrub, the cold wind off the high peaks. They will call her Dihya, the gazelle, for a swiftness that will one day outrun every army sent against her, though the invaders who come after will give her a colder name of their own.
suggested_refs: Ibn Khaldūn's Kitāb al-ʿIbar, the genealogy 'Dihya bint Tabīta' that opens her legend
sources: Talbi's alternate genealogy, 'Dihya daughter of Matiya son of Tifian'
Keuter, The Contested Legend of al-Kâhina (UCLA thesis, 2019)

stops.name: The Aurès, the Jarawa remember three faiths for her
stops.campa: The tribe that raises her keeps its own memory of God, and later ages will not agree on what it was. Some call the Jarawa Judaized Berbers, keepers of a law carried north when Israel's kingdom reached toward Syria; others find in the martyrs' graves near Theveste the mark of Christian Numidia, and place a wooden image, perhaps a cross, in the girl's household before she ever lifts a sword; still others say the mountain never stopped honoring its own old gods of sun and stone. The register sets down all three, as the Aurès itself does, and chooses none.
suggested_refs: The Judeo-Berber theory of Nahum Slouschz, resting on a single Ibn Khaldūn passage
The martyrdom of Saint Crispina at Theveste (Tébessa), on the Aurès' own doorstep
sources: Roth, 'The Kâhina: Legendary Material in the Accounts of the Jewish Berber Queen' (1982)
Hendrickx, 'Al-Kâhina: The Last Ally of the Roman-Byzantines' (2013)

stops.name: The Aurès, the gift comes on her
stops.campa: Before Islam ever crosses into Ifriqiya, the mountain already calls her kahina: not yet a name but an office, the one who sees. The chroniclers who will write of her in Arabic centuries hence describe an ecstatic seized by her own gift: she beats her breast, her unbound hair stands on its own, and out of the seizure comes true knowledge: of enemies not yet arrived, of years not yet lived. The Jarawa bring her their disputes the way they once brought them to their fathers' oracles, and she answers. What she does not yet know is what she is being prepared to answer for.
suggested_refs: The prophetess-type she shares with Deborah, with Cassandra, and with Fatma n'Soumer after her
sources: Norris, The Berbers in Arabic Literature (1982)

stops.name: The Aurès hears of Vescera
stops.campa: Word climbs the mountain roads that a Berber king named Kusayla has done what no one thought possible: ambushed the Arab conqueror ʿUqba ibn Nafiʿ near Vescera, in the Biskra flats below, and killed him beside his own rival Abu al-Muhajir. Kairouan, the Arabs' new city, empties before him; Kusayla enters it a king. The Jarawa of the Aurès are not his tribe, but the news is every mountain clan's news alike: that the invader can be made to bleed. Dihya, grown now into the tribe's oracle, hears it as everyone hears it, and marks how briefly such victories tend to last.
suggested_refs: The site of ancient Vescera, modern Biskra

stops.name: Kairouan, Kusayla's brief kingdom
stops.campa: For some five years the Christian Berber king holds the Arabs' own capital, ruling from Kairouan over a realm that reaches, they say, from Volubilis to the Aurès, the first time since Jugurtha that a Berber crown sits so wide. The Jarawa watch from their mountains, neither wholly his subjects nor wholly free of the current he has started. Dihya, whom the tribe already brings its hardest questions to, reads in Kusayla's reign the shape of something not yet finished: a war the Arabs have only paused, waiting on their own civil wars in Damascus to end before they come back for it.
suggested_refs: The Great Mosque of Kairouan, held briefly under a Berber king

stops.name: The valley of Mamma, east of Timgad: Kusayla falls
stops.campa: The Umayyads, their own house settled, send Zuhayr ibn Qays back into Ifriqiya with fresh men. Outnumbered in the valley the Aurès country calls Mamma, east of the Roman ruins of Timgad, Kusayla's Awraba companies are broken and their king is killed. The mantle of resistance he carried for five years falls into the mountain with no one yet to lift it. Refugees from the valley climb into Jarawa country carrying the news, and, the tradition says, carrying Kusayla's own bones, for he will be buried at last at Khenchela, in ground the Aurès itself keeps.
suggested_refs: The ruins of Roman Timgad, UNESCO World Heritage, beside the valley of Mamma

stops.name: The Aurès, the Zenata turn to Dihya
stops.campa: With Kusayla dead and Zuhayr himself soon cut down by Byzantine raiders on his own road back to Barqa, the resistance in Ifriqiya has no head. The Zenata confederation, the Jarawa first among them, turns to the woman the mountain already calls its seer. She is no man's wife to be set aside, no king's daughter waiting on a throne; she is acclaimed the way the mountain has always chosen its leaders, by the weight the tribes already give her word. From the Aurès to the salt flats of the Hodna, chiefs who fought under Kusayla now swear themselves to Dihya.
suggested_refs: The Zenata confederation's tribal unity, later read into the Imazighen flag's blue, green, and gold
sources: Norris, The Berbers in Arabic Literature (1982)

stops.name: The Aurès: sons, and the household of the priestess-queen
stops.campa: In the years of gathering strength, sons are born to her: Yamin, some tellings say, of a Berber father, and another son, by a different account, of Greek or Byzantine blood; the chroniclers cannot agree, and the register keeps both readings side by side rather than choose between them. She rules a household as she will soon rule a confederation, her authority resting on the same gift that first made the tribe bring her its disputes. Widowed, or never remarried, she raises her sons in a camp already arming, and does not yet tell them what one day she will ask of them, because she does not yet fully know it herself.
suggested_refs: The disputed genealogies of her two sons, Berber and Byzantine, kept side by side in the chronicles
sources: Hendrickx (2013), on the 'probable' element of two sons

segments.name: Baghaya, and the Coming of Hassan

stops.name: The Aurès hears of Carthage, taken and retaken
stops.campa: Far to the east a new general, Hassan ibn al-Nu'man al-Ghassani, lands in Ifriqiya, takes Carthage, and pushes the Byzantine exarchate toward the sea. Then, in 697, the emperor Leontios's fleet retakes the city, and Hassan falls back on Kairouan to regroup. Twice now the news has run up the mountain roads to the Aurès: first that the great Roman city has fallen, then that it has not. Dihya reads both messages the same way: that the Arabs will come for the mountain next, whichever way Carthage falls, and that the Aurès had better be ready before they do.
suggested_refs: The Byzantine exarchate of Carthage, in its last years of nominal Roman rule
sources: Hendrickx (2013), on the Byzantine retaking of Carthage in 697

stops.name: Baghaya, the town brought down by her own order
stops.campa: Fearing that Hassan will fortify Baghaya as a forward base against the Aurès, Dihya orders the town demolished before he can reach it: walls, granaries, the market that has fed her own people for generations. It is the first stroke of a policy she will carry much further before the war ends: better ash than an enemy's citadel. The people of Baghaya obey a queen they do not yet resent, though the register does not hide what this costs them, or how the debt of it will be called in later, when the towns tire of losing everything twice over.
suggested_refs: The modern town of Baghaï, Khenchela Province, rebuilt on the razed site

stops.name: The Aurès, the Zenata host gathers
stops.campa: From every valley of the confederation the men come armed to Dihya's camp: Jarawa spearmen, Zenata horse, whatever is left of Kusayla's old Awraba companies, Byzantine stragglers who would rather die under a Berber banner than none at all. She reviews them the way the tradition says she reviews everything: by instinct and by the sight that is not quite sight, walking the ranks and marking, though she tells no one yet, which faces she expects to see again and which she does not. Hassan is coming up from Kairouan with the largest army the Aurès has ever had to answer.
suggested_refs: The confederation muster as later imagined in Amazigh national art and mural

stops.name: The Wadi Miskiana, the river named before the battle
stops.campa: The armies close on the river the country will afterward call wadi al-balaa, the river of the ordeal, or, in the Arabs' own record, wadi Nini, the name settling on the ground before the fighting even starts, as though the land itself already knows how the day will go. Dihya makes her dispositions along the banks with the confidence of someone who has already seen the field empty of the enemy. Her captains, less certain, watch the far bank where Hassan's much larger host is making its own camp, cookfires lighting the whole opposite shore by evening.
suggested_refs: The modern town of Meskiana, Oum el Bouaghi Province, on the historic river
sources: Meskiana battle accounts per Talbi (cited in Keuter, 2019)
medievalists.net, 'The Berber Queen who defied the Caliphate'

stops.name: Wadi Miskiana: the battle, and Hassan broken
stops.campa: The battle that follows is total. Dihya's Zenata horse, Kusayla's veterans, and whatever discipline five years of resistance has taught them together break the largest army the Umayyads have yet sent into Ifriqiya. Hassan himself barely escapes the field; his dead are left for the Aurès to count, and the survivors do not stop retreating until they have put the whole of Tripolitania between themselves and the mountain. For the first time since the Arabs crossed into Ifriqiya, no Muslim army stands anywhere between the Aurès and the sea. The Jarawa's oracle has become, in a single afternoon, the ruler of the Maghreb.
suggested_refs: The battle remembered today in Amazigh commemorations of the mountain's great victory
sources: medievalists.net, 'The Berber Queen who defied the Caliphate'

stops.name: The wind changes on the wasted ground
stops.campa: In the pursuit that follows, the tradition remembers a second cruelty of the land turned to her purpose: fire set loose on the wind into the dry country the retreating Arabs must cross, denying them forage, water drawn from wells already fouled, any harvest left to seize. Whether it is Dihya's own order or the common practice of any army living off a wasted land in that age, the chroniclers lay it at her name, as they will lay the whole of the coming policy at her name. Hassan's remnant reaches Cyrenaica half-starved. The Maghreb, for five years now, will answer to no one else.
suggested_refs: The scorched fields between the Aurès and Tripolitania, remembered as her first great ash

stops.name: Kairouan, abandoned: the Arabs fall back to Cyrenaica
stops.campa: Hassan does not stop at Tripolitania; word reaches the Aurès that he has gone all the way back to Cyrenaica to wait on the Caliph's own reinforcements, ceding even Kairouan for a season to whoever will hold it. Dihya does not occupy the Arabs' capital, the register is careful to say her interest is the mountain and the confederation, not Arab cities, but for five years no Muslim garrison west of Barqa can call itself safe. It is the high mark of the whole resistance, Kusayla's and hers together, and it will not come again.
suggested_refs: The interregnum of c. 698-701, the longest stretch Ifriqiya goes without a Muslim army

stops.name: The Aurès, mistress of the Maghreb, mountain to Ghadames
stops.campa: For five years, the tradition's own count, Dihya rules as the uncontested power of the Maghreb, her word running from the high Aurès out across the pre-Saharan oases as far as Ghadames. She holds no Arab city and builds no new capital; her throne is the mountain itself and the confederation's own councils. Chiefs who fought under Kusayla and chiefs who never did now answer alike to the seer of the Jarawa. It is the only stretch in the whole Arab conquest of North Africa when the invasion simply stops, turned back by a woman the enemy's own chroniclers will not be able to leave out of their histories.
suggested_refs: Ghadames oasis, the western limit later ascribed to her rule

stops.name: The order of fire, the towns and the orchards
stops.campa: The Arabs, she is certain, seek not faith but plunder: gold, silver, the wealth of settled towns. Dihya extends the logic of Baghaya's ruin into policy: orchards cut down, granaries burned, walled towns leveled from the edge of Tripolitania toward Tangier, so that no invasion will find anything worth the risk of returning for. It is remembered as her most terrible order and her most contested: later historians will ask whether any single ruler commanded so vast a devastation, or whether the Arabs' own scorched earth, well attested elsewhere in their conquests, was afterward laid at her name instead of theirs.
suggested_refs: The disputed scale of the scorched-earth order, weighed against Rome's own precedent at Carthage

stops.name: The Aurès: an envoy from Hassan, and the answer she gives
stops.campa: From Tripolitania Hassan sends terms before he sends soldiers: submission, tribute, the peace an occupying power always offers before it has the strength to take by force what it asks for. Dihya hears the envoy out in full council, the same gift that reads battlefields now reading the offer for the weakness inside it: a general without an army, buying time from a queen who does not yet know she is running out of it. She sends the envoy home with her answer and nothing else: the Maghreb from the mountain to Ghadames already has a ruler, and does not need a second.
suggested_refs: The thinly attested diplomatic exchange of the interregnum years

stops.name: The camp on the border, Khalid ibn Yazid taken and adopted
stops.campa: Among the Arab officers her forces take, one, Khalid ibn Yazid al-Qaysi, she does not send back with the rest. In the tribe's own rite of milk-kinship she has him fed from her own hand, barley meal worked with oil, the bsisa of adoption, and sets him beside her own sons. She tells them the words the tradition keeps: he is one of them now. An Arab prisoner is made a Berber son by a Berber mother, kept at her right hand for the five years of her reign, learning her camp and her counsel as no other Arab is permitted to.
stops.quote_source: al-Raqīq al-Qayrawānī's account of the milk-kinship adoption, as carried in Kahina (en.wikipedia)
suggested_refs: The Berber custom of adoption by nursing (bsisa), still practiced in the Aurès into the modern era
sources: Roth (1982), on Khalid's introduction to the narrative

stops.name: The Aurès, the towns grow weary of ash
stops.campa: What wins the mountain does not win the plain. Farmers and townsfolk who have lost orchard after orchard, market after market, to a policy meant to starve out an enemy who has not yet returned, begin to count what the war has cost them against what it has bought. Some now send word, quietly, toward Hassan's camp in the east: better an Arab peace than another year of the Kahina's fire. Dihya's own gift does not fail her here: she reads the drift in her councils before it becomes open defection, but reading it and reversing it are not the same power.
suggested_refs: The sedentary-nomad divide E.-F. Gautier later reads as the whole meaning of her story

stops.name: The Aurès, word that the Caliph is sending an army
stops.campa: From Damascus the Caliph Abd al-Malik ibn Marwan, his own house secure after the long civil wars, answers Hassan's request with the men and money the Aurès victory had denied him for five years. New troops march west out of Egypt; defectors from the Berber confederation itself go over to swell Hassan's ranks. Dihya's own scouts bring the count into her camp long before the army arrives, and she reckons it honestly against what five years of ash have left her to meet it with. The gift that once read only enemies now reads her own arithmetic, and it does not favor her.
suggested_refs: The Umayyad Caliphate under Abd al-Malik ibn Marwan, its civil wars settled at last

stops.name: The Aurès, the dream of the head
stops.campa: The tradition keeps one vision above all the others she is said to have had: that she sees her own head cut away and carried east, laid down before the great king of the Arabs in his own city, proof sent across the whole breadth of the Maghreb that the Kahina's war is over. She does not hide the vision from her sons or from Khalid; she tells them plainly what is coming, the way she has told the tribe plainly every true thing her gift has ever shown her. What she asks of them because of it, she has not yet asked, but the shape of the asking is already set.
suggested_refs: The prophecy of her own death, which Brett and Fentress read as 'the whole purpose of her existence' in the earliest Arabic accounts

stops.name: The Aurès, she sends her sons and Khalid to Hassan
stops.campa: Before the armies close for the last time, Dihya calls her sons and her adopted Khalid to her and tells them what the dream has already told her: go to Hassan's camp, not hers; take the faith that is coming whether she wins or not; live, and let the line survive the mother. She releases Khalid at last into the purpose she raised him for, and sends her own sons with him. It is read afterward two ways at once: a mother's mercy, and a queen's last act of statecraft, binding her people's future to the enemy's mercy before the enemy has even won.
stops.quote: I adopted you for this day.
stops.quote_source: al-Raqīq al-Qayrawānī's account of the sending of the sons, as carried in Kahina (en.wikipedia)
suggested_refs: The sons' later commands under the very general who killed her, read by Brett and Fentress as 'a celebration of the alliance of the two nations'

stops.name: The Aurès, the last muster
stops.campa: She arms for a battle she has already told her own household she expects to lose. The confederation that answered her five years running answers her again now, thinner than it was, some chiefs gone over to Hassan, some towns unwilling to burn a second time, but the Jarawa core and what remains of Kusayla's old companies still take the field under her standard. She rides as she has always ridden, hair loose in the old manner of the seer going to battle, sons and adopted son already sent ahead into the enemy's keeping, so that whatever the day brings, it brings it to her alone.
suggested_refs: The image of the loose-haired warrior-queen, later compared by Norris to Boudica and to Queen Asbyte of the Garamantes

segments.name: Gabès, and the Well of the Queen

stops.name: Gabès, the last defeat
stops.campa: The armies meet near Gabès, on the coastal road where the Numidian kings once held their salt-lake frontier, and this time Hassan's reinforced host does not break. Whole companies of her own confederation, worn down by five years of scorched fields, either fail her in the field or have already gone over; one telling even preserves an old officer of Kusayla's own line fighting now against her. Dihya's line is broken by evening. She does not surrender the field; she leaves it, riding for the only ground left that has never betrayed her: the Aurès itself.
suggested_refs: The Numidian salt-lake frontier at Gabès, held since the age of Masinissa
sources: Roth (1982), citing Abun-Nasr on the Gabès engagement

stops.name: The retreat road, 'monarchs do not flee from death'
stops.campa: On the road back into the mountain her own captains beg her to keep riding, to scatter into country too broken for Hassan's cavalry to follow, to live. She refuses in the words the tradition keeps as her last recorded defiance: she is a queen, and queens do not run from death. She turns her diminished companies to make what stand the ground allows, choosing the manner of the end over the postponement of it, the same clarity, the register insists, that let her read every battlefield for five years now turned at last upon her own.
stops.quote: How can I leave and flee when I am a queen? Monarchs do not flee from death, and how can I bring shame upon my people for all eternity?
stops.quote_source: al-Zāwī's account of her refusal to retreat, as carried in Kahina (en.wikipedia)
suggested_refs: The last stand read against Boudica's, and against Fatma n'Soumer's a millennium later in the same mountains

stops.name: Bir al-Kahina, the well that keeps her name
stops.campa: Hassan's cavalry runs her companies down in the borderland between the Aurès and the desert, at a well the country will call Bir al-Kahina from this day on and still calls it now, thirteen centuries later. The chroniclers do not agree on the manner of the end: sword in hand, most say; some say by her own poison rather than capture, but they agree she is killed there and beheaded on the spot, the well becoming the one fixed point the whole disputed legend can be hung from. The Aurès has lost its oracle and its queen in the same afternoon.
suggested_refs: Bir el Ater, Tébessa Province: the well still carrying her name into the present
sources: Roth (1982), citing Ibn Khaldūn's placement of her death at the Well of al-Kahina

stops.name: Damascus, the head before the Caliph
stops.campa: Her head is carried the whole width of the conquest, from the Aurès to Damascus, and laid before Caliph Abd al-Malik ibn Marwan as the promised proof that the Kahina's war is finished, the very scene, the tradition insists, that she had already seen in her own dream and had already told her sons was coming. Whether the Caliph receives it as triumph, or, as some later tellings soften it, as the melancholy proof of an enemy worth respecting, the register does not choose. What the whole Maghreb now knows is that the mountain's five years are over, and the invasion, delayed as long as one woman could delay it, resumes.
suggested_refs: The Umayyad court at Damascus under Abd al-Malik ibn Marwan, receiving the proof of the last resistance broken
sources: Battle of El Jem / Battle of Tabarka (en.wikipedia)

stops.name: Kairouan, the sons received
stops.campa: Hassan welcomes her sons and her adopted Khalid exactly as the dream foretold: not as hostages but as officers, converted and commissioned, given command over Berber troops within the very army that killed their mother. It is remembered two ways at once, as the register keeps both: a conqueror's shrewdness, binding the defeated confederation to himself through her own blood, and the fulfillment of a mother's last calculation, that her line and her people would outlast her by joining what she could not defeat. Twelve thousand Berbers, some from her own confederation, are enrolled under the new peace.
suggested_refs: The 12,000 Berber levies raised from the defeated confederation, the army's new backbone

stops.name: The Straits, her people's sons cross into Iberia
stops.campa: Eight years after her death, Berber troops raised from the very confederations she once led cross the narrow water under Tariq ibn Ziyad, the rock where he lands keeping his own name into the present, Jabal Tariq. Some tellings go further and make Tariq himself her kinsman, even her son, by another accounting, a claim the register cannot confirm but records as part of what the legend has grown to hold. Whatever the truth of that claim, it is her people's spears, not the Arabs' alone, that open Spain, the last irony of a war she fought to keep them free of any empire at all.
suggested_refs: Jabal Tariq / Gibraltar, named for the Berber general some legends bind to her own line
sources: Maddy-Weitzman, The Berber Identity Movement and the Challenge to North African States (2011), on the Tariq-as-kinsman legend

stops.name: Kabylia, Lalla Fatma n'Soumer takes up the mountain's old office
stops.campa: More than eleven centuries on, the mountains answer a second time to a woman the country calls prophetess. Lalla Fatma n'Soumer leads the Kabyle resistance against a new invader, the French, from strongholds in the Djurdjura ranges that once sheltered the Aurès confederation's western kin; it takes an army of thirty thousand to put her down in 1857. The register does not claim her as Dihya's blood, only as the mountain's habit: that when North Africa's plain surrenders, its highlands produce, again, a woman who will not.
suggested_refs: Lalla Fatma n'Soumer, held by the French until her death in exile, buried at El Djazair
sources: Ait Frawsen & Ukerdis, 'The Origins of Imazighen Women's Power in North Africa' (2003)

stops.name: Baghaï, the statue raised, burned, and mended
stops.campa: In 2003, on the same ground she once ordered razed, the Association Aurès El-Kahia raises a statue of Dihya in Baghaï's town square, the queen remembered exactly where the queen once burned a town for her people's sake. On the night of 12 April 2016 unnamed arsonists set the statue alight, a small violence answering a larger argument still unresolved: whose heroine she is, and what her memory is for. Within days young Chaoui from the mountain restore her, unasked: the same local devotion that first kept her name alive when no chronicle would.
suggested_refs: The Baghaï statue, burned and restored within days by the town's own young people
sources: lematindz.net, 'La statue de la reine amazigh Dihya incendiée à Baghaï'
Becker, 'The Kâhina: The Female Face of Berber History' (2019)

stops.name: Tizi Ouzou: the mural, and the name still spoken
stops.campa: On a wall outside Tizi Ouzou, in the heart of Kabylia, a mural sets Dihya beside Massinissa and Jugurtha, three Imazighen resisters, one of them a woman, claimed together as the deep root of a people the Arabic chronicles once tried to erase and the French colonial pen once tried to annex for its own argument. The Amazigh flag she is painted beside, blue for the sea, green for the mountain, yellow for the desert, the red tifinagh letter for the free man at its center, flies now over a living movement that reads her, still, as its oldest face.
suggested_refs: The Imazighen flag; the Tizi Ouzou mural photographed by Cynthia Becker, 2006
sources: Becker, 'The Kâhina: The Female Face of Berber History' (2019)
